title: DoorDash's $17B Acquisition of Instacart Points to a World Without Employees
author: Lee Hepner
content:
Today, news broke that food delivery company DoorDash bought its rival
Instacart for a reported $17 billion. The deal is slated to close in early
2028, which means the two companies understand it is going to receive
significant antitrust scrutiny, even under the Trump administration. According
to Reuters this morning, review is
[likely](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/doordashs-instacart-deal-
may-draw-ftc-scrutiny-amid-cost-of-living-concerns-2026-10-29/) to fall under
the ambit of the Federal Trade Commission, which separately launched an
[inquiry](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-
launches-personalized-pricing-compensation-inquiry) this week into an array of
companies -- including both DoorDash and Instacart -- for alleged surveillance
pricing. And there's a reason the acquisition may face tough regulatory
hurdles, which I'm going to get into.

But the more important question involved in this merger is what it says about
how we understand the nature of work, and how the goal is to unravel a social
contract we put together in the late 19th century about our relationship with
big business. Both Instacart and DoorDash are leaders in the "gig economy,"
both in terms of shaping the legal terms and in encouraging corporate America
elsewhere to try and turn their workforce into temporary or gig workers, which
is akin to "piece work" during early industrialization.

[![DoorDash to Acquire Instacart For $17
Billion](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cMrW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F26734bf8-8245-4277-84b0-2ecc3898acc4_738x415.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cMrW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F26734bf8-8245-4277-84b0-2ecc3898acc4_738x415.jpeg)

We'll start with the merger. Here's
[Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-29/doordash-to-
buy-instacart-in-17-billion-deal):

> DoorDash Inc. agreed to buy rival Instacart in a deal that values the
> company at about $17 billion, the latest sign of consolidation in an
> increasingly competitive delivery market where Walmart Inc. and Amazon.com
> Inc. loom large.
>
> For DoorDash, which is already the leading restaurant delivery app in the
> US, buying Instacart will boost its grocery delivery segment, which co-
> founder and Chief Executive Officer Tony Xu recently described as the
> fastest-growing part of the business. The merger would likely help DoorDash
> tap older users, who tend to use Instacart more to order groceries, analysts
> from TD Cowen wrote Thursday.
>
> The deal would also better position DoorDash to compete with retail giants
> like Walmart and Amazon, which have made online grocery orders a bigger
> priority and rely on their own apps.

This combination would significantly reshape the delivery space, which is a
big part of how American consumers interact with business. And it met with
vehement and instant political opposition. Here's the Mayor of New York City:

### What Is DoorDash?

DoorDash is the dominant platform-to-consumer delivery service for restaurants
in the United States, with an estimated [67%
share](https://secondmeasure.com/datapoints/food-delivery-services-Grubhub-
uber-eats-DoorDash-postmates/) of the domestic market by monthly sales. At
this point, DoorDash and Uber Eats are really the only two competitors here,
comprising about [90%](https://secondmeasure.com/datapoints/food-delivery-
services-Grubhub-uber-eats-DoorDash-postmates/) of the market, after DoorDash
[acquired](https://www.eater.com/2019/8/1/20750912/doordash-buys-caviar-food-
delivery-app-410-million) Caviar in 2019 and Uber Eats
[acquired](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/05/technology/uber-postmates-
deal.html) Postmates in 2020. (Uber Eats also made a play for Grubhub in 2019,
but abandoned it, and now Grubhub is bottoming out.) And that's just the
domestic restaurant delivery market. DoorDash has also expanded
internationally, through its [acquisitions](https://ir.doordash.com/news/news-
details/2022/DoorDash-Completes-Acquisition-of-Wolt/default.aspx) of Wolt, and
last year's $3.7 billion [acquisition](https://ir.doordash.com/news/news-
details/2025/DoorDash-Completes-Acquisition-of-Deliveroo/default.aspx) of
Deliveroo.

I live in San Francisco where all of these companies started, working on the
city council as part of the early regulatory response to insulate restaurants
from commissions that were [pushing
30%](https://www.sfgate.com/food/article/restaurants-doordash-delivery-
commission-fees-17769734.php). Suddenly I was receiving emails from two
lobbyists instead of four, because the consolidation had actually sapped the
market for lobbyists.

The consolidation coincided with the intervening COVID-19 pandemic, which
super-charged platform-to-consumer delivery services. The 2020 boom in online
delivery made sense, as delivery platforms transformed overnight into
essential services, and delivery drivers became _de facto_ front line workers.
And that accelerated adoption of online food delivery has hardly waned. Today,
the percentage of Americans who dine out with regularity continues to fall,
while the percentage of Americans who regularly use platforms like DoorDash
and Instacart has steadily
[increased](https://news.gallup.com/poll/716090/ordering-groceries-online-
fewer-dining.aspx).

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SuAh!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe97fc6fc-
da04-4503-ae48-88a3e4c60601_792x376.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SuAh!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe97fc6fc-
da04-4503-ae48-88a3e4c60601_792x376.png)

So that's DoorDash. What about its dance partner, Instacart?

### What Is Instacart?

Instacart is the most dominant third party grocery delivery service in the
country, with an estimated share of about
[57.7%](https://www.emarketer.com/content/instacart-retail-advertising-
partnerships-2025). Instacart's domination of the third party grocery delivery
market [includes](https://company.instacart.com/pressreleases/new-economic-
impact-report-quantifies-instacarts-role-as-grocery-industry-growth-engine-
and-job-creator) over 2,200 brands and 100,000 grocery stores reaching 98% of
homes in the country. And according to their recent SEC quarterly
[filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1579091/000157909126000042/cart-20260630.htm),
they're active in the restaurant delivery space, too, meaning they are a
direct, if nascent, competitor to the entity acquiring them.

In other words, this combination is more than a merger of compliments, with
shared back-end operations, it's also a merger between direct competitors
across groceries, restaurants, and delivery drivers.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TB9u!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9edf265e-6cbe-41f4-864a-5fac84390818_755x426.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TB9u!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9edf265e-6cbe-41f4-864a-5fac84390818_755x426.png)

### The Case for the Merger

Of course I'm skeptical of this merger, but is there a case _for_ the
combination? Well, Instacart and DoorDash would argue they are little fish in
a big pond, and dispute the high market shares. As to Instacart, their
substantial market share is in third party grocery delivery services, which
they could claim aren't a real market. What about something like Walmart or
Amazon, which offers direct delivery? A lot of people shop at Walmart, and
Walmart can crowd Instacart out of the market with free delivery and other
promotions. These would be, according Instacart/DoorDash, real competition.

That said, this counter-argument misses a key problem. Restaurants and
independent grocers must use third party delivery services, they simply don't
have the scale or brand that Kroger, Amazon, or Walmart have. So at least for
them, third party delivery is a real market. And these independents have
already been
[complaining](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/FTC-2026-0463-0224) about
having to fork over their competitively sensitive information and trade
secrets.

The consumer side is another area to examine; both DoorDash and Instacart are
under a new microscope for [potential](https://www.ftc.gov/news-
events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-launches-personalized-pricing-
compensation-inquiry) surveillance pricing, as of just yesterday. If their
data scales the ability to personalize pricing, then we might see the kind of
direct evidence for market power that is anathema to a merger.

What makes this merger so interesting is that the harms are more likely to
affect suppliers, namely restaurants, drivers and delivery workers, and
grocery stories. And in this respect, it is a story of the combined firm's
buyer power, and it is a _labor_ story. Historically, labor has not really
been part of the antitrust legal approach, because labor law and antitrust
have existed in separate legal arenas. But as big corporations have taken
apart the very notion of the employee, through
[misclassification](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/misclassification)
and the broader phenomenon of the "fissured workplace," the distinction
between antitrust and labor law is collapsing.

### **The Rise and Fall of the Employee**

To understand what this merger says about how you and I work, consume, or buy,
let's rewind the clock about 125 years. The way we generally think about work,
and the relationship between employers and workers, took shape during the
sweeping industrialization of the economy in the late 19th and early 20th
Century. Older forms of work were characterized by skilled artisans and family
farms. From the 1890s to the 1910s, big employers gained control over
production, costs and labor - a factory-based model of production - while
workers fought for higher wages, shorter hours, and a voice in the workplace.

Here's Woodrow Wilson in 1913 [describing](https://constitutioncenter.org/the-
constitution/historic-document-library/detail/woodrow-wilson-the-new-
freedom-1913) the change that happened in most people's memories:

> We have come upon an age when we do not do business in the way in which we
> used to do business,--when we do not carry on any of the operations of
> manufacture, sale, transportation, or communication as men used to carry
> them on. There is a sense in which in our day the individual has been
> submerged. In most parts of our country men work, not for themselves, not as
> partners in the old way in which they used to work, but generally as
> employees--in a higher or lower grade--of great corporations. There was a
> time when corporations played a very minor part in our business affairs, but
> now they play the chief part, and most men are the servants of corporations.

It would be too simple to characterize the old order as fundamentally
independent and egalitarian -- there was no shortage of exploitation taking
place among farm workers -- but generally speaking workers had much more
control over their productive labor. The rise of factories led to greater
specialization of skills, workplaces became more centralized, and there was a
new dependence formed between employers and their workers.

This period also saw the emergence of two bodies of law - antitrust and labor
- which developed on mostly separate but parallel tracks, and not without
conflict. In 1886, the American Federation of Labor
[formed](https://www.loc.gov/collections/american-federation-of-labor-
records/articles-and-essays/timeline/) to represent some 140,000 skilled
tradesmen in their pursuit of better wages and working conditions, and they
engaged in strikes and collective bargaining to do so. Meanwhile, lawmakers
sought to control corporate power with new laws like the Interstate Commerce
Act in 1887, which regulated railroad prices and prohibited discrimination,
and the nation's foundational, enduring antitrust law, the Sherman Act in
1890.

Labor unions and antitrust laws sought to address the abuse of corporate power
in different ways. But when Senator John Sherman railed against "a king over
the production, transportation, and sale of the necessities of life," and AFL
President Samuel Gompers declared, "You are our employers, not our masters,"
it was two sides of the same coin.

But in the early years, enforcers used the Sherman Act
[against](https://lawreview.uchicago.edu/print-archive/restructuring-american-
antitrust-law-institutionalist-economics-and-antitrust-labor) organized labor
to restrain labor strikes and boycotts. That friction created a persistent and
lasting discord. Even after the Clayton Act of 1914 explicitly exempted the
combination of workers from the Sherman Act, courts construed the exemption
narrowly and continued to
[enjoin](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/254/443/) certain types
of boycotts and strikes. Two decades after the Clayton Act, Congress passed
the National Labor Relations Act in 1935, amid a depression, militant labor
organizing, greater federal intervention in the economy, and collective
bargaining emerged as the preferred means of countering employer power and
abuses.

In the traditional employer-employee relationship, the fundamental exchange
went as follows. Employees received a living wage, or salary, and benefits in
return for employer control over the labor of the individual. The conflict
between labor and capital, then, was premised on the ability of workers to
organize for better pay. This deal was a narrowing of earlier labor goals,
such as the Knights of Labor, who wanted sovereignty over production, but it
did foster broadly shared wealth.

Since the 1970s, even this narrower deal unraveled, with offshoring, union-
busting, immigration policy, and a decline in the minimum wage, among other
statutory changes to employee power. Anyone interested in a deeper narrative
should go pick up _[How Antitrust Failed
Workers](https://www.ali.org/news/articles/how-antitrust-failed-workers)_ by
Eric Posner, a 2021 book which follows the rise of labor, and its decline
beginning in the 1970s. Posner's broader point was that antitrust was meant
originally as a pro-labor doctrine, to prevent concentrations of capital from
dominating Americans. Enforcers and judges, however, so perverted the law that
we simply created an entirely separate legal regime for industrial labor,
forcing large corporations to take responsibility for their employees in a
variety of ways.

And Posner argued, as have many over the past decade, that should change.
Shortly after publishing it, Posner joined the Biden Antitrust Division, and
actually enacted many of the ideas in his book.

Under the Biden administration, enforcers sought to explicitly deal with power
in labor markets in a number of ways, seeking to
[ban](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/noncompete-rule) non-
compete agreements, bringing [criminal
charges](https://www.legal500.com/intelligence/united-states/antitrust-
competition-law/doj-brings-first-criminal-antitrust-charges-for-wage-fixing-
and-no-poach-agreement-between-employers) against employers colluding to wage-
fix, [blocking](https://www.npr.org/2022/11/01/1133032238/judge-blocks-
penguin-random-house-simon-schuster-merger) the Penguin/Simon and Schuster on
author wage grounds, and successfully
[challenging](https://www.economicliberties.us/press-release/ftc-and-states-
block-kroger-albertsons-in-historic-win-for-competition-and-communities/) the
Kroger-Albertsons merger on the grounds the combined entity would have more
bargaining power over workers and labor unions.

These moves were not just creative, but indicated that the economy has
structurally changed such that employers have become big enough to exert
market power over wage-setting, even as the definition of the employee had
been eroded for decades. Labor law alone, beleaguered by decades of eroded
union membership, just could no longer deliver.

### **A World Without Employees**

And with that, let's get back to DoorDash's proposed acquisition of Instacart.
Under the hood of this transaction is a new wave of tech- and platform-based
gig work, which breaks the traditional employment relationship that has
existed for over a century.

Today, many companies use platform-based gig work, where an employer can
control every facet of work, while absolving themselves of the obligation to
provide a consistent wage and benefits. In theory, workers can choose when
they want to work and earn some supplemental income. In
[practice](https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2026/article/exploring-the-
complexities-of-nonstandard-employment-the-2022-23-california-work-and-health-
survey.htm), over 1.1 million Californians, comprising 81% of all app-based
gig workers, consider it their main job. And it's not just delivery and
rideshare drivers, everyone from
[nurses](https://rooseveltinstitute.org/publications/uber-for-nursing/) to
[software engineers](https://www.hrw.org/report/2025/05/12/the-gig-
trap/algorithmic-wage-and-labor-exploitation-in-platform-work-in-the-us) are
becoming app-based gig workers. By at least one estimate, [over
half](https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/McKinsey/Industries/Retail/Our%20Insights/Automation%20in%20retail%20An%20executive%20overview%20for%20getting%20ready/Automation-
in-retail-An-executive-overview-for-getting-ready-FINAL.pdf) of the United
States workforce could be gig workers by 2027.

The campaign to institutionalize this form of exploitation has been
extraordinary. In early 2020, Instacart was found
[liable](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/first-judge-rules-instacart-
has-misclassified-its-california-workers-n1142286) for worker
"misclassification," in the wake of a California Supreme Court decision,
called _[Dynamex](https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-
court/2018/s222732.html)_ , that established a three-part test for whether an
employment relationship was subject to employee protection laws. Later that
year, Instacart and DoorDash would end up contributing a
[combined](https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_22,_App-
Based_Drivers_as_Contractors_and_Labor_Policies_Initiative_\(2020\)) $83
million to Proposition 22, a California statewide ballot measure that
overturned the California Supreme Court and the state legislature's same
[codification](https://www.smithcurrie.com/publications/california-law-
notes/ab5-dynamex-the-abc-standard-and-their-effects-on-the-construction-
industry/) of the three-part test.

Altogether, over [$204
million](https://www.latimes.com/business/technology/story/2020-11-13/how-
uber-lyft-doordash-won-proposition-22) was spent by gig companies, including
Uber and Lyft, to preserve the independent contractor model. Until this year's
billionaire wealth tax, it was the most expensive political campaign in
California history.

![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uAKv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61cf4816-cdba-4b6c-993e-88c19ccc9e55_936x297.jpeg)

The gig-ification of work has had expectedly deleterious effects for worker
compensation. A 2022
[study](https://www.nationalequityatlas.org/research/analyses/prop-22-pay-
study) following the adoption of Prop 22 found that median take-home earnings
were just $6.20 per hour. Because gig workers only get paid for when they are
working a job, and not while they are waiting or in transit for a gig, they
aren't paid for their total time, further diminishing what they would make as
employees. According to the same 2022 study, the post-Prop 22 wage floor was
just $4.10, nearly $10 lower than the state's minimum wage. California workers
received [less](https://laborcenter.berkeley.edu/gig-passenger-and-delivery-
driver-pay-in-five-metro-areas/) compensation than their counterparts in five
other metros.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-VoG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3602d9aa-8a34-4275-8255-9fc366a14970_936x344.png)

And gig employers, like Lyft and Uber who pull a lion's share of the weight
for their industry counterparts, including DoorDash and Instacart, have
threatened capital strikes to keep it that way. In 2024, Uber and Lyft
[threatened](https://apnews.com/article/minneapolis-uber-lyft-ridehailing-
minimum-wage-d60db6a2e2580dc1d93c438a8cffa5ee) to leave Minneapolis over the
state's new minimum wage law, and at that point, I noted the moral question at
hand.

It was a bluff; a dozen competing rideshare firms began [lining
up](https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/uber-and-lyft-alternatives-say-
they-will-launch-minneapolis-soon-just-not-today) to take the mantle from Uber
and Lyft, in full compliance with Minneapolis law. The ability to introduce
more competition, which is often frowned upon by certain corners of the left
as some sort of brutal struggle, was in this case going to lead to higher
wages.

[![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dz4n!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2ee7359b-c4ea-4f3f-bb14-e130bcd6a6ad_648x347.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dz4n!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2ee7359b-c4ea-4f3f-bb14-e130bcd6a6ad_648x347.jpeg)

Nevertheless, Democratic Minnesota state lawmakers backed down, negotiating a
[deal](https://www.fox9.com/news/uber-and-lyft-say-they-will-stay-in-
minnesota) to reduce minimum driver pay from Minneapolis' $1.40 per mile and
51 cents per minute, to a statewide $1.27 per mile and 49 cents per minute.

Yet another layer is the ability of gig platforms to deploy [wage
discrimination algorithms](https://columbialawreview.org/content/on-
algorithmic-wage-discrimination/), capable of surveilling workers and pricing
their labor based on any number of factors. Here's a Reddit post that went
viral last year, posted by someone who was presumably employed by the
corporate office of a gig company, describing how pay was allocated pursuant
to a driver's "Desperation Score."

[![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fMtj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F87a1958b-90b3-454b-b70d-904960c3b1d5_936x801.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fMtj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F87a1958b-90b3-454b-b70d-904960c3b1d5_936x801.jpeg)

### The Real Goal of DoorDash-Instacart

It should be clear at this point that DoorDash and Instacart built their
business models on the premise that the traditional obligations to employees
could be jettisoned by turning them into gig workers. That extra cost, in the
forms of higher wages, liability insurance, health care, and so forth, is
profit to the platform as human beings were classified as "independent
businesses."

And now comes the second stage, an important source of scrutiny for regulators
reviewing the DoorDash-Instacart deal, which is the roll-up of market power
over gig workers, along with the potential extraction from independent
restaurants and grocers. The two
[platforms](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1792789/000179278926000013/dash-20251231.htm)
[combined](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1579091/000157909126000018/cart-20251231.htm)
"employ" about 9.6 million drivers, but compensation terms vary, and some gig
workers engage in "multi-homing" or "[multi-
apping](https://www.nelp.org/app/uploads/2021/11/App-Based-Workers-Speak-
Oct-2021-1.pdf)," using multiple platforms simultaneously to optimize for
better gigs. One analysis of the two platforms
[reveals](https://www.worksolo.com/blog/instacart-vs-doordash-driver-pay)
different pay structures and promotional offers between the two platforms,
resulting in different overall compensation ($16 on Instacart, $15 on
DoorDash) and per-order tips ($5 on Instacart, $3 on DoorDash). There are also
special compensation terms unique to grocery shopping, to account for [heavy
baskets](https://company.instacart.com/shoppers/shopper-earnings) and the time
it takes to do the actual shopping. It's unclear how all of those compensation
terms would be consolidated into a single app, but collapsing competition
between these two platforms risks reducing the ability of gig workers to "bid"
up compensation by pitting utilization of each platform against the other.

These important dynamics aside, the relationship between platforms and workers
is a fundamentally new way to understand the social contract. It is not a
return to pre-industrial norms, because large corporations didn't exist then,
but they do now. It is something relatively new, having emerged over the past
15 years. Or at least, it _could_ be something new. This path ahead is not
pre-determined. And the point of the history lesson on antitrust and labor is
that the path forward could and should look like a unity of interests aimed at
re-balancing this asymmetric power dynamic.

We're seeing the signs of it. The new Biden-era antitrust policy on labor,
continued [oddly](https://search.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-
releases/2025/09/ftc-takes-action-protect-workers-noncompete-agreements) in
[narrow ways](http://search.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-
releases/2025/12/ftc-continues-enforcement-action-streak-against-
anticompetitive-no-hire-agreements) by Trump, is a key part of it. Laws have
also been introduced in several states and federally not just to prohibit
surveillance pricing, but also to
[prohibit](https://casar.house.gov/media/press-releases/news-congressman-greg-
casar-introduces-new-stop-ai-price-gouging-and-wage) surveillance wage
discrimination. It's the reflection of a populist form of politics that is
appearing at the local level, too, and the Mamdani Administration is a highly
visible part of that work. Last month, NYC Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice
Julie Su and Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Commission Sam
Levine -- both former Biden Administration officials -- led a [$131.5
million](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dca/news/065-26/mayor-mamdani-wins-
record-131-5-million-doordash-delivery-workers) enforcement action against
DoorDash. And DoorDash issued its own press release, leading with: "[We
screwed up](https://about.doordash.com/en-us/news/dcwp)."

There's another approach that draws on price fixing law, and the interesting
wrinkle here is that the push by gig platforms to classify their workers as
independent contractors could expose them to liability for fixing the wages of
independent competitors. In California, recently-passed Assembly Bill 325
[prohibits](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/ab-325-shared-
pricing-algorithms-liability-california.html) any use of a common pricing
algorithm to coerce the setting of prices on independent businesses. Well,
independent contractors are technically independent businesses, a "wage" is
the price of labor, and there's nothing more coercive than a take-or-leave
price.

I've used the DoorDash-Instacart acquisition to talk about the need for a
renewed, dual commitment to antitrust and labor, because this $17 billion
proposed acquisition is the next data point in the restructuring of American
life. And as gig work expands to other sectors, it's not hard to see a lot of
dead canaries in the coal mine over the past 15 years.
